candidates.attacker_control: The `callback` (or `c`) HTTP query parameter on GET requests to the SockJS transport paths (e.g. `<sockjs-mount>/<server>/<session>/jsonp` or `/htmlfile...`). The value is fully attacker-controlled and is not restricted by the route regexes, which only constrain the path segments, not query parameters.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Searched the whole repository for any callback validation: no CALLBACK pattern or identifier whitelist exists (the only `[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]*` regex is RouteImpl's path-token regex, unrelated). Verified `escapeForJavaScript` is applied only to SockJS frame bodies (BaseTransport.java 94-102) and never to the callback. Verified the transports are enabled unless explicitly disabled (SockJSHandlerImpl.java 131-141; SockJSHandlerOptions.disabledTransports defaults to an empty set, SockJSHandlerOptions.java 44/50-56). Verified the value is taken from the decoded query parameters and written to the response without an intervening filter. Counterargument considered: JSONP by design echoes a callback name, so reflection itself is expected; the defect is the absence of identifier validation, which turns the reflection into script injection (and the htmlfile variant is directly navigable text/html). Mitigations exist but are opt-in (disabling transports, deploying a restrictive CSP), not defaults.
candidates.impact: Reflected cross-site scripting in the origin of the Vert.x web application for any victim that opens the crafted URL or loads it as a script. This allows arbitrary JavaScript execution in the victim's authenticated context: theft of non-HttpOnly cookies and page data, reading of CSRF tokens, forging authenticated requests/actions, and content/credential phishing. Because the JSONP/HTML-file endpoints are unauthenticated and enabled by default whenever a SockJSHandler is used, the attack needs no prior session and no user interaction beyond visiting the link.
candidates.prerequisites: An application registers a SockJSHandler (documented usage: `router.route("/eventbus/*").handler(SockJSHandler.create(vertx).bridge(...))` or `socketHandler(...)`) and does not explicitly disable the JSON_P / HTML_FILE transports (default: enabled). The endpoint requires no authentication; a victim must follow a crafted link or load the endpoint in a browser script/iframe context. `SockJSHandlerOptions.setInsertJSESSIONID` or session state does not affect reachability, because BaseTransport.getSession creates a fresh SockJSSession for unknown IDs.
candidates.root_cause: The SockJS transport handlers take the `callback` (fallback `c`) query parameter from the request and concatenate it unvalidated into a response that the browser parses as executable content. JsonPTransport.JsonPListener.sendFrame builds `callback + "(\"" + body + "\");"` and serves it as `application/javascript`; HtmlFileTransport substitutes the callback into its HTML template (`var c = parent.{{ callback }};`) and serves it as `text/html`. Only the SockJS frame body is passed through `escapeForJavaScript` (BaseTransport.escapeForJavaScript, StringEscapeUtils.escapeJavaScript); the callback is never validated or escaped (no callback/identifier pattern exists anywhere in the repository). The transports are registered by default: SockJSHandlerOptions.disabledTransports starts empty and SockJSHandlerImpl.socketHandler only removes explicitly disabled transports, so Transport.JSON_P and Transport.HTML_FILE are active in the default configuration.
candidates.title: Reflected XSS via unvalidated SockJS callback parameter in JSONP and HTML-file transports
candidates.trace: HTTP GET -> SockJSHandlerImpl.handle (line 85-90) -> internal router -> JsonPTransport route handler reads `rc.request().getParam("callback")` (JsonPTransport.java 62-69) -> `new JsonPListener(rc, session, callback)` (line 75) stores the raw string (line 139) -> `session.register(req, listener)` (SockJSSession.register, lines 279-319) -> `writeOpen(lst)` (line 301/403-405) -> `TransportListener.sendFrame("o")` -> JsonPListener.sendFrame (lines 144-165) emits `callback("o");` with Content-Type `application/javascript; charset=UTF-8`; the htmlfile transport follows the identical route (HtmlFileTransport.java 90-102 -> 114-118 -> 121-136) and substitutes the callback into the `<script>` block of a `text/html` document at line 124. Indexed call edges (JsonPTransport constructor -> SockJSSession.register; JsonPListener -> sendFrame) are consistent with this source-level trace but are navigational only.
candidates.unverified: No runtime execution, HTTP request, tests, or scanners were run; browser execution and exact byte output were not observed. Exploitability for a given deployment depends on the application actually mounting a SockJSHandler and leaving JSONP/HTML-file transports enabled; no such deployment code was executed. The relation index provides no data-flow or reachability proof, so the trace is source-level only.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting'); injection of attacker-controlled data into a JavaScript/HTML response without validating it as a JavaScript identifier

coverage_summary: Source scope reported 244 files (211 Java, plus Kotlin, JS, HTML/XHTML resources, XML/POM) with binary files skipped by policy; the relation index covers all 244 files with 0 parse errors, 3014 symbols, 5434 edges, but explicitly has no control-flow, data-flow, or semantic resolution and reports 4841 unresolved calls. I reviewed in depth: vertx-web routing/path core (RouterImpl, RouteImpl, RoutingContextImpl/Base/Wrapper, Utils), the full sockjs package (SockJSHandlerImpl, JsonPTransport, HtmlFileTransport, XhrTransport, EventSourceTransport, WebSocketTransport, RawWebSocketTransport, BaseTransport, SockJSSession, SockJSSocketBase, EventBusBridgeImpl, BridgeOptions/options classes), auth/security handlers (AuthHandlerImpl, AuthorizationAuthHandler, BasicAuthHandlerImpl, DigestAuthHandlerImpl, RedirectAuthHandlerImpl, OAuth2AuthHandlerImpl, JWTAuthHandlerImpl, FormLoginHandlerImpl, CSRFHandlerImpl, SessionHandlerImpl, SessionImpl), StaticHandlerImpl, CORsHandlerImpl, ErrorHandlerImpl, LoggerHandlerImpl, TemplateHandlerImpl/CachingTemplateEngine and several template engines, CookieImpl, HeaderParser/ParsableHeaderValue, vertx-web-client core (WebClientImpl, HttpRequestImpl, HttpContext, BodyCodec), and parts of vertx-web-api-contract (OpenAPI3RouterFactoryImpl, SecurityHandlersStore, BaseValidationHandler). Examples and documentation sources were skimmed. Not exhaustively reviewed: all template-engine-specific implementations, the remainder of vertx-web-api-contract validators/openapi3 internals, Kotlin sources, the two bundled JS clients, and HTML/XML resources; the relation index provides only syntactic navigation, so absence of an indexed relation is not evidence of absence of code.
limitations: No code was executed, no tests or scanners were run, and no HTTP requests were made; the finding is source-level and not runtime-confirmed.

The P1 index is syntactic/navigation-only (no control flow, data flow, or semantic resolution, 4841 unresolved calls); it was used to trace candidate call edges but every edge cited here was re-checked against source text.
Exploitability is deployment-dependent: it assumes an application mounts a SockJSHandler without disabling the JSONP/HTML-file transports.
I could not confirm how a browser/HTTP stack renders the crafted response in this specific Vert.x version, and no CSP or reverse-proxy behavior (which could mitigate) was inspected.
Windows-specific StaticHandler behavior could not be validated, and other unreviewed files may contain additional issues not reflected in the single candidate submitted.

rejected_leads.lead: ErrorHandlerImpl renders `{errorMessage}` and `{stackTrace}` into a text/html error page without HTML escaping (ErrorHandlerImpl.java 115-128, 122-128).
rejected_leads.reason: Only reachable with `displayExceptionDetails=true` (not the default), and the message is normally server-generated exception/status text rather than direct request input; attacker control is indirect and configuration-dependent, so it is weaker than the SockJS callback reflection.

rejected_leads.lead: StaticHandlerImpl may allow directory traversal on Windows via backslash separators (`%5c`) because `Utils.removeDots` only treats '/' as a separator (StaticHandlerImpl.java 138, 611-615; Utils.java 172-231).
rejected_leads.reason: Platform-specific and unconfirmed; on Unix-like systems the decode/remove-dots sequence neutralizes the tested single- and double-encoded dot-dot forms, and no Windows behavior can be verified here. Not selected as the single strongest candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: OAuth2AuthHandlerImpl redirects to the unvalidated `state` parameter after the callback (OAuth2AuthHandlerImpl.java 185-221), an open-redirect-style behavior.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires a valid OAuth2 authorization code exchange and a configured callback route; the redirect target is echoed from the provider round-trip and the practical impact/attacker control is weaker and more conditional than the unauthenticated SockJS reflection.

rejected_leads.lead: DigestAuthHandlerImpl nonce counter (`nc`) check/update is not synchronized (DigestAuthHandlerImpl.java 119-127) and uses non-constant-time/hash-based nonces.
rejected_leads.reason: Only a narrow replay/race window for an already-authenticated client, and the nonce map is per-handler; no source evidence of a concrete authentication bypass, so it does not meet the evidence threshold.

rejected_leads.lead: BaseTransport.setCORS reflects the request Origin with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` (BaseTransport.java 155-167) and setJSESSIONID echoes request cookie content back in Set-Cookie (130-153).
rejected_leads.reason: This is the SockJS protocol's cross-domain design, and the cookie echo is limited to a `JSESSIONID`-prefixed request header fragment with CRLF rejected by the HTTP/1.x header parser; no concrete impact demonstrated beyond the intended behavior.

rejected_leads.lead: LoggerHandlerImpl logs the Referer/User-Agent header values unsanitized (LoggerHandlerImpl.java 112-125), enabling log forging.
rejected_leads.reason: Log injection has low security impact and appears to be upstream-intended behavior; not a candidate for the strongest finding.

rejected_leads.lead: StaticHandlerImpl directory listing inserts file names/paths into HTML without escaping (StaticHandlerImpl.java 650-688).
rejected_leads.reason: The injected content is server filesystem names, not request-controlled data; lower attacker control and requires a hostile filename on the server.

summary: Review of the vertx-web snapshot (244 files, 211 Java; parent version 3.5.3.CR1). I inspected the security-relevant code paths: routing/core (RouterImpl, RouteImpl, RoutingContextImpl(Base/Wrapper), Utils path normalization), auth handlers (Auth, Basic, Digest, Redirect, OAuth2, JWT, AuthorizationAuthHandler), session/CSRF/CORS/static/error/logger/template/favicon/virtual-host handlers, the entire SockJS package (handler, transports, session, bridge), vertx-web-client core, and parts of vertx-web-api-contract. The strongest distinct candidate is a reflected XSS in the SockJS JSONP and HTML-file transports: the attacker-controlled `callback` (or `c`) query parameter is embedded verbatim into JavaScript/HTML responses. Both transports are enabled by default and the endpoint is reachable without authentication, so a victim visiting a crafted URL (or embedding it as a script) executes attacker JavaScript in the application's origin. Other plausible but weaker issues are listed as rejected leads. No runtime execution, tests, or scanners were used; conclusions are source-level.
